slides: This is the table the raters use to score the content of your essay.
So first, the big picture. And then, lesson by lesson, we'll go deep into each part.
Two raters read your essay. Each one gives content a score from one to six, and language a score from one to six.
And these two are scored separately. Great English doesn't save weak content... and the other way around.
So what do they look at in content? Here's what the official guide says, in short.
Keep this list in mind. Everything in the next lessons comes back to one of these questions.
Now, I'll be honest with you. The detailed wording in the table doesn't really help us.
For critical thinking, for example, it says: very impressive, impressive, adequate, insufficient, very little.
Well, what's impressive? What's very little? You have nothing to compare it to.
A rater who has read thousands of essays knows exactly what impressive looks like. But you and I can't use that.
So we'll focus on the criteria themselves. The left column of the table. What exactly is being checked.
The content table has four rows.
One, the main idea and the central thesis. Is it relevant to the task, and is it well supported?
Two, development of the thesis. Are the explanations full, and are the arguments convincing and varied?
Three, focus and coherence. Does one idea lead to the next, without jumps, and without repeating yourself?
Each row goes from one, very poor, to six, very good. A lot of the time no description fits perfectly, so the rater picks the closest one.
In our lessons we'll call them relevance and the main idea, development, focus and coherence, and critical thinking. Each one gets its own lesson... starting now.
